title: Pricing brainstorm: per job or per technician
scratchpad:
brainstorm only, nothing decided
per job (Greta) vs per tech (Marcus)
names floated: Crew/Depot/Network, Solo/Shop/Enterprise
interviews first
segments: This is a brainstorm, not a decision meeting. Atlas is still only a codename, and I want ideas for how next year's plans could be priced before anyone gets attached to numbers.
Good. I'd like to hear the wild options too. Nothing we say today goes anywhere near a website.
Today everyone pays the same: one plan, twenty four dollars per technician per month. It's simple, but a big fleet and a tiny shop pay exactly the same rate.
The problem I keep seeing is that technicians are a bad proxy for value. A shop doing forty jobs a day gets far more out of us than one doing five.
So my wild option is pricing per completed job. Charge a small amount every time a job is marked done. Our revenue grows when our customers grow.
Per job scares me. Customers would hesitate to log small jobs in the app just to keep the bill down. We'd be punishing exactly the usage we want.
And forecasting gets harder for them. A dispatcher can tell you how many technicians they have. Nobody knows how many jobs they'll do in March.
That's fair. A hybrid, then? A base per technician, and a small per job fee above some monthly volume?
Hybrids look clever in a spreadsheet and confuse everyone on a pricing page. I'd rather have tiers where each step up includes more.
Let's hear tiers, then. Marcus, how many, and what would separate them?
Three. A basic one for self-serve shops, a middle one with the scheduling smarts, and a top one for big fleets that comes with a sales conversation.
What counts as the smart stuff? Route optimization?
Route optimization, reporting, maybe a customer portal one day. The basic tier would be the app and the dispatch board, and nothing else.
I like that the expensive features also cost us more to run. So the tiers would line up with our costs as well as with value.
Names? I know it's early, but names shape how people think about a tier.
I've been playing with Crew, Depot and Network. Crew for a small team, Depot for a business with a base, and Network for multi-site fleets.
Those are a bit cute for me. I'd go plainer: Solo, Shop and Enterprise. Nobody has to think about what they mean.
Enterprise sounds expensive before anyone has seen a price. That might be good or bad, depending on who's reading.
We're not picking names today. Write them all down, and we test them with customers.
Price points? Even rough ones, just so we know the shape?
I'd rather not put numbers on tiers before we know what's in them. Every number we say today will end up anchoring the debate next year.
Agreed. Let's get the packaging right first and price it after the interviews.
What about the competition? Do we know how the others charge?
Roughly. Most of the field service apps we compete with charge per technician. Nobody we know of charges per job, which is either an opportunity or a warning.
Probably a warning. But it's worth testing before we rule it out completely.
Okay. The next step is interviews. Who can set them up?
I'll ask the sales team for ten customers who'd talk to us, a mix of small shops and larger fleets.
And I'll pull a sample of a hundred accounts and compare what they'd pay per technician with what they'd pay per completed job, just to see how far apart the numbers land.
I'll put the tier sketch and all the name options on one page, so the interviews have something concrete to react to.
Good. To be clear for the notes: no decisions today. No pricing model, no names, no prices. We come back to this after the interviews, early next year.

items.text: Price next year's plans per technician, per completed job, or a hybrid? Brainstorm only, no decision
Compare per-technician and per-job pricing on a sample of a hundred accounts
Line up ten customer interviews through the sales team
